source.title: A Closer Look at Memorization in Deep Networks
source.authors: Devansh Arpit; Stanislaw Jastrzebski; Nicolas Ballas; D. Krueger; Emmanuel Bengio; Maxinder S. Kanwal; Tegan Maharaj; Asja Fischer; Aaron C. Courville; Yoshua Bengio; Simon Lacoste-Julien

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some plotted results do not have recoverable numerical values in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests noisy-label learning and regularization, and argues that networks learn shared patterns before memorizing noise. Its results refine the random-label memorization claim by showing slower memorization under regularization and different learning dynamics on real and noisy data.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. for perfect fitting of pure noise; cited results are not recorded as this study’s results. Own results include noisy-label accuracy curves, regularization effects, and training-dynamics measurements. Figures 7–11 are described but their plotted values are not available as exact numbers in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own comparisons of learning on real and noise data, noisy-label learning dynamics, and regularization effects. It qualifies claims about memorization and originates V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that SGD-trained networks prioritize shared patterns before memorizing noise, that tuned regularization can slow memorization while preserving clean-data generalization, and that effective capacity depends on the data as well as architecture and training procedure.
record.recipe_differences: Builds on Zhang et al.’s noise-dataset methodology; adds measurements of learning dynamics, critical-sample ratios, capacity, training time, and regularization. This paper is an original source for V6.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise fraction affects final and maximum validation accuracy; regularization type affects the degree to which random-label memorization is hindered, with dropout reported as most effective.

fits_no_version.finding: Gaussian-input-noise datasets show greater sensitivity of convergence time to dataset size and capacity than real datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimization cost of fitting unstructured inputs depends strongly on capacity and dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: Critical-sample ratios and loss-sensitivity distributions differ between real and noise data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Real and noise data produce different decision-boundary complexity and example-influence distributions.

record.problems: Several relevant outcomes are presented only in figures, with no exact values or uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. The paper does not provide a separate text-reported outcome for fitting a completely random labeling to zero or near-zero error under unchanged settings.

untested.parts: The supplied text does not establish the complete conjunction of near-zero error on fully random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
A small constant-factor overhead for random labels and convergence slowing with increasing label corruption are not established. Figure 6 varies Gaussian input corruption.
Shuffled pixels and independently permuted pixels are not tested.
The full zero-to-total label-corruption sweep, perfect training fit at each level, and the chance-performance endpoint are not recoverable from the supplied results.
Data augmentation, eventual fitting after arbitrarily longer regularized training, and the effect of removing regularizers on true-label generalization are not established.

missing.what: Gaussian-input fitting to 100% training accuracy and its dependence on capacity and dataset size; extract the tested conditions without inventing numerical convergence times.

Fully random-label training accuracy for the zero-regularization baseline and individual regularization settings. Figure 10 contains directly relevant measurements, but their values cannot be recovered here.
Training-loss trajectories showing that regularizers change memorization speed differently from learning speed on real data.

record.verdict_notes: This study is the original source for V6, so no V6 verdict is assigned. Its original-source status for V6 does not exclude verdicts on V3–V5, whose originating source is Zhang et al. Missing figure values are evidence gaps, not evidence that an effect is partial or absent.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies random labels, but its own stated results here do not report a recoverable outcome for fitting a completely random labeling to zero or near-zero training error under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters. The pure-noise fitting result is attributed to Zhang et al.
The figures cover 20% to 80% noisy labels, not a stated continuous sweep from none to all; exact accuracy values are not stated in the text.

The paper studies regularizers while training on random labels and evaluating generalization on clean data. It does not report the separate claim that removing regularizers by itself makes true-label generalization poor.

The paper tests mixed real and noisy labels and describes validation accuracy peaking before training accuracy becomes high. It does not report a direct comparison of representations or a complete account of the learning order for every noise level.

rows.subject: CNNs
rows.operation_detail: Train on CIFAR-10 with 20% to 80% of training labels replaced by random labels; measure train and validation accuracy.
rows.measure: Training and validation accuracy during training
rows.note: The text states that for randY, maximum validation accuracy occurs before training accuracy becomes high, and that noisier datasets have lower final and maximum validation accuracy. Exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The text explicitly reports lower final and maximum validation accuracy with increasing label noise, and validation accuracy peaking before high training accuracy. These observed components do not establish perfect final training accuracy or a full sweep to chance.

rows.subject: CNNs
rows.operation_detail: Train on CIFAR-10 with random labels under dropout; compare random-label training accuracy and clean validation accuracy across dropout settings.
rows.measure: Final training accuracy on randY versus best validation accuracy on clean CIFAR-10
rows.value: Figure only; text says dropout is the most effective regularizer for hindering memorization.
rows.note: The authors report that dropout can hinder memorization without reducing the model’s ability to learn; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: The original observed state reverses the implication for V5: tuned dropout reduces random-label training performance while preserving clean-data generalization. The authors characterize this as slowing memorization; permanent prevention is not established. Clean validation accuracy comes from separately trained clean-data models.

rows.check: Dropout with adversarial training hinders memorization while preserving clean-data learning, qualifying V5 rather than supporting it. This concerns finite-training performance and speed, not demonstrated impossibility of eventual fitting. Clean-data results use separate models.
